csKnowledge: n-gram tokenization of CAD operation sequences
TF-IDF style idiom-frequency ranking across joined corpora
pass1.buildNote: Mine idioms from BOTH Inventor and SolidCAM corpora jointly — joined frequency must outvote single-source noise, and dedup idioms by canonical operation signature.

pass2.systemImpact: The joined idiom corpus feeds downstream CAD-automation strategy selection (CADActionValidationEngine U-DASAL15 verifies actions against mined idioms, and the MS1 dispatcher cascade U-DASAL16 surfaces idioms to consuming CAM dispatchers). If joined frequency is computed wrong, single-source noise propagates as 'best practice' into every downstream strategy recommendation. CAMK and CAM-EXHAUST cross-CAM synthesis later assume this idiom store is canonical.
csDepth: Joined-corpus mining is a stratified-counting problem: a raw global Apriori run lets the larger corpus dominate support thresholds — normalize support per-source or weight by inverse corpus size before merging, else the rule set is just the bigger corpus.

n-gram tokenization of operation sequences must canonicalize parameter-bearing operations (a Drill@10 and Drill@12 are the same idiom) — without an equivalence class on the token alphabet the itemset lattice explodes and idioms never reach minimum support.

csKnowledge: result-receipt chaining (verify each step's actual output, not its return code)
idempotent re-verification of a completed action
pass1.buildNote: Verify each CAD action by reading its ACTUAL produced geometry/state, never the call's return code — fail loud and name which action failed (R12).

pass2.systemImpact: This is the verification gate the entire CADCAM-DAGI pipeline depends on — every CAD action emitted by the idiom learner and the MS2 feature engines passes through it before CAM consumes the geometry. If it regresses to checking return codes instead of actual state, a failed feature operation silently produces a wrong solid that the CADCAMHandoffEngine (MS7 U-DAE2E03) then certifies, and CAM cuts the wrong part. It is a precondition for CADValidationGateHook (MS3 U-DACAV09).
csDepth: Result-receipt chaining is a provenance problem: each action must emit a receipt referencing the prior receipt's hash, so a verifier can detect a skipped or reordered step — a flat per-action boolean cannot catch a dropped intermediate operation.

Idempotent re-verification requires the verifier to be a pure function of observed geometry/state, never of mutable side-channel counters; re-running verify on an already-completed action must be a no-op that returns the same verdict — otherwise concurrent re-checks race.

csKnowledge: feature-cascade fan-out wiring to every consuming dispatcher
pass1.buildNote: Wire every MS1 engine to ALL dispatchers that would naturally consume it (not just one) in the same commit; the z.enum(ACTIONS) gate must list every new action or production breaks while tests false-pass.

pass2.systemImpact: This unit is the wiring choke point for all of MS1 — the idiom learner and CADActionValidationEngine become invisible to the rest of PRISM until their actions are registered on prism_cadautomation and fanned out to prism_cam. A missed action enum entry means production 500s on that action while MockMCPServer-based tests false-pass (the documented z.enum bypass class). Every later milestone's dispatcher-wiring unit (MS2 U-DACFS14 ... MS7 U-DAE2E08) repeats this pattern and inherits the same hazard.
csDepth: The action enum is a single shared mutable surface across many milestones — concurrent wiring units in different chats race to append to the same z.enum array; the round-trip E2E must assert against the real SDK-validated boundary, not the mock, or the regression is invisible.

Feature-cascade fan-out is a graph-reachability obligation: every dispatcher that transitively consumes the engine's output must be wired in the same commit — a partial fan-out leaves an orphan path that the stop_on_unwired_assets hook should catch but only if the engine has zero refs, not one-of-N.

csKnowledge: NURBS surface lofting along multiple rail curves
bidirectional spline interpolation across guide rails
pass1.buildNote: Multi-rail sweeps must keep the section curve perpendicular to ALL rails simultaneously — verify continuity (G1/G2) at every rail intersection with a known analytical surface.

pass2.systemImpact: AdvancedSweepEngine is a primitive geometry producer — its surfaces feed BoundarySurfaceEngine (U-DACFS03), MultiBodyManagementEngine (U-DACFS08), and ultimately the BRep validator (MS3 U-DACAV01). A non-G1/G2-continuous rail join silently produces a surface the manifold checker later rejects, stalling the whole MS2→MS3 handoff; CAM toolpath generation on a defective swept surface gouges.
csDepth: Multi-rail synchronization is a reparameterization problem: rails of different arc-length must share a common parameter domain — chord-length or centripetal reparameterization, not uniform knot spacing, or the section curve drifts and twists along the sweep.

Knot-vector merging across rails has quadratic blow-up risk: naively unioning all rails' knot vectors multiplies control-point count; knot removal with a bounded deviation tolerance is required to keep the surface tractable for downstream tessellation.

pass1.buildNote: Loft across N profiles must resolve point-correspondence consistently — mismatched profile point counts twist the surface; verify against the single-profile wing-loft baseline.

pass2.systemImpact: AdvancedLoftEngine produces skinned surfaces consumed by the same MS2 downstream chain (boundary, multi-body) and validated by MS3's BRep/dimensional gates. A twisted loft from bad point-correspondence produces a geometrically wrong solid that passes a naive area check but fails manifold validation — corrupting the CAD→CAM handoff. Shares the NURBS engine dependency with U-DACFS01.
csDepth: Profile-to-profile correspondence is an assignment problem: minimize total point-pair distance (Hungarian algorithm) or align by arc-length parameter — a greedy nearest-neighbor match twists the surface when profiles have different orientations.

Mismatched profile point counts force a resampling decision before lofting; resampling to the LCM or to a fixed dense sampling trades control-point bloat against fidelity — pick the resampling density from a continuity-error budget, not arbitrarily.

csKnowledge: Coons / Gordon patch construction from N boundary curves
boundary curve closure and tangency continuity checks
parametric surface fitting to bounding edge loop
pass1.buildNote: An N-boundary surface requires a closed, non-self-intersecting edge loop — validate boundary closure and edge-to-edge tangency before fitting; a non-watertight boundary silently produces a degenerate patch.

pass2.systemImpact: BoundarySurfaceEngine closes edge loops into surfaces consumed by MultiBodyManagementEngine and the MS3 manifold validator. A non-watertight boundary that silently yields a degenerate patch is the exact defect class the BRep validator (U-DACAV01) exists to catch — but a degenerate patch can pass Euler-characteristic checks while being unmachinable, so the failure must surface here, not three engines downstream.
csDepth: Boundary closure detection is a graph-cycle problem on the edge-loop topology: verify every edge endpoint has degree 2 and the loop is a single cycle before fitting — a figure-eight or open chain must fail loud, not produce a self-intersecting Coons patch.

Coons vs Gordon patch choice depends on boundary count and whether interior curves exist; a 4-boundary case is bilinearly-blended Coons, N>4 needs a Gordon surface or triangulation — picking the wrong constructor for the boundary count yields visible cross-boundary discontinuity.

pass1.buildNote: T-spline/SubD synthesis must handle extraordinary (star) vertices without surface creasing — verify limit-surface continuity with a known control cage.

pass2.systemImpact: FreeformSurfaceSculptEngine produces T-spline/SubD surfaces that must be convertible to NURBS or tessellated for the MS3 validators and CAM. A creased limit surface at a star vertex passes BRep manifold checks but produces a CAM gouge — so SubD continuity must be verified at sculpt time. Feeds the same MS2 multi-body and MS3 validation chain as the other surface engines.
csDepth: Catmull-Clark subdivision at extraordinary vertices does not converge to C2 — only C1 with bounded curvature; the engine must classify star points and either apply a special tuned subdivision mask or flag the region, never assume uniform C2.

SubD-to-NURBS conversion for downstream CAD interop is lossy near star points; carrying a tolerance budget through the conversion and failing loud when it is exceeded prevents a silently-degraded surface reaching CAM.

csKnowledge: directed-acyclic dependency graph of parametric rules
pass1.buildNote: Parametric rules form a dependency DAG — topologically sort before evaluation and fail loud on cycles; a circular driver rule must not silently loop.

pass2.systemImpact: ParametricDriverEngine orchestrates rule-driven parametric updates that re-drive part geometry — it is the automation layer the parametric-part-library and assembly engines depend on for design-intent propagation. A circular driver rule that silently loops hangs the CAD pipeline; a wrong topological order applies rules with stale inputs, producing geometry that the MS3 dimensional validator then flags as out-of-spec without explaining why.
csDepth: Rule evaluation requires cycle detection on the dependency DAG (Tarjan/Kahn) before any forward-chaining pass — a cycle must fail loud naming the rule chain, never be broken arbitrarily, since either break point produces different geometry.

Forward-chaining over a DAG must handle the diamond-dependency case: a rule reachable by two paths must evaluate exactly once after both predecessors settle — memoize on rule identity, not on invocation, to avoid redundant re-fires that thrash dependent geometry.

csKnowledge: boolean solid operations (union/subtract/intersect) on multi-body parts
pass1.buildNote: Multi-body management must track each body's solid topology independently and detect shared faces — boolean ops between bodies must preserve manifold validity.

pass2.systemImpact: MultiBodyManagementEngine is the consumer of every MS2 surface/solid producer (sweep, loft, boundary, sculpt) — it composes them into multi-body parts that AssemblyConstraintEngine (U-DACFS09) and the MS3 validators operate on. A boolean op that breaks manifold validity corrupts the body graph and every downstream interference check; a missed shared-face produces a false collision report in U-DACAV06.
csDepth: Boolean solid ops are numerically fragile at near-coincident faces: a robustness epsilon and exact-arithmetic predicates (orientation tests) are needed, or union/subtract produces sliver faces that break manifold validity intermittently.

Body-graph adjacency tracking is an incremental-update problem — each boolean op must locally patch the adjacency structure rather than rebuilding it, and shared-face detection must use spatial hashing on face bounding boxes to avoid the O(n^2) all-pairs comparison as body count grows.

csKnowledge: constraint solver for assembly mates (DOF reduction)
pass1.buildNote: Each mate/joint removes specific DOFs — over-constrained assemblies must be detected (DOF < 0), and motion joints must produce kinematically valid travel envelopes.

pass2.systemImpact: AssemblyConstraintEngine reduces assembly DOF and solves kinematic chains — its output feeds AssemblyInterferenceValidatorEngine (MS3 U-DACAV06) for collision checks through motion envelopes and the BOM synthesis engine for the assembly tree. An undetected over-constrained assembly (DOF<0) silently locks geometry; a wrong motion envelope makes the interference validator miss a collision in a configuration the part actually reaches.
csDepth: DOF counting must respect redundant constraints: naively summing per-mate DOF removal over-counts when two mates constrain the same axis — a constraint Jacobian rank computation gives the true mobility (Grübler's formula is only an upper bound).

Forward kinematics on a closed kinematic loop is not a simple chain product — closed loops need a constraint-solver (Newton iteration on the loop-closure equations); a chain-only solver silently produces a non-closing assembly.

csKnowledge: structural frame member generation along skeleton edges
miter / coped joint trim geometry at frame intersections
pass1.buildNote: Weldment frames sweep a profile along a skeleton — joint trimming (miter/cope) at member intersections must produce no gaps or interference; never inline structural-steel constants.

pass2.systemImpact: WeldmentFrameGeneratorEngine produces structural frame geometry whose joints feed the MS3 manifold/interference validators and whose strength is checked against the bolted-joint and weld-strength engines. A miter/cope trim that leaves a gap produces a non-watertight solid the BRep validator rejects; inlined structural-steel constants are the exact CALC-HARDEN bug class that the canonical-constants enforcer (U-CH16) blocks.
csDepth: Joint trimming is a pairwise solid-boolean problem at every skeleton-edge intersection — the trim order matters when 3+ members meet at a node; a deterministic precedence (by member size or priority) is needed or the trimmed geometry is non-deterministic.

Sweeping a cross-section along a skeleton edge requires a stable frame (rotation-minimizing frame, not Frenet) to avoid section twist at inflection points — a Frenet frame flips at zero-curvature spans and twists the member.

csKnowledge: orthographic projection of 3D model to 2D views
ASME Y14.5 GD&T symbol/datum placement rules
pass1.buildNote: Technical drawing synthesis must place GD&T feature-control frames and datums per ASME Y14.5 grammar — verify projection consistency across all generated views.

pass2.systemImpact: TechnicalDrawingSynthesisEngine emits ASME Y14.5 drawings from the MS2 solid models — these drawings are the GD&T spec source the MS3 DimensionalValidatorEngine (U-DACAV02) compares actual geometry against, and PrintIngestEngine (MS7) round-trips. A wrong feature-control-frame placement or inconsistent projection makes the dimensional validator measure against a wrong datum, cascading a false out-of-spec verdict.
csDepth: Hidden-line removal is an O(n^2) edge-vs-face occlusion problem; a BSP-tree or depth-sorted painter approach is needed for tractability, and the view consistency check must ensure the same 3D edge is hidden/visible coherently across all orthographic views.

GD&T symbol placement is grammar-constrained: feature-control-frame composition (tolerance | datum-A | datum-B) follows Y14.5 ordering rules — a placement engine that emits frames without validating the datum-reference grammar produces drawings that humans and the dimensional validator interpret differently.

pass1.buildNote: BOM generation must recursively walk the assembly graph, roll up quantities of identical components, and emit a stable schema-versioned record.

pass2.systemImpact: BOMiPropertySynthesisEngine flattens the assembly graph into a BOM consumed by ERP/inventory engines and the OptimalMachineSelectorEngine (MS7) for shop-floor routing. A wrong quantity roll-up under-orders stock; a non-schema-versioned record breaks the ERP consumer on the next schema bump. It depends on the assembly graph being correct (built by U-DACFS08/09).
csDepth: Recursive assembly-tree traversal must detect shared sub-assemblies (DAG, not tree) — a pure tree walk double-counts a component used in two sub-assemblies; memoize visited sub-assembly nodes and multiply quantities along the path.

Quantity roll-up de-duplication needs a stable component-identity key (part number, not object reference) — iProperty metadata normalization must canonicalize before the roll-up, or the same physical part appears as two BOM lines.

pass1.buildNote: Every MS2 surface engine must be wired to all consuming dispatchers in one commit; the action enum must include each new action or production is broken while MockMCPServer tests false-pass.

pass2.systemImpact: This wiring unit makes the 9 MS2 surface/assembly/drawing engines reachable from prism_cadautomation and fans them out to prism_cam — until it lands, all of MS2 is built-but-orphan. A missed action enum entry 500s production while mock tests pass. MS3 validators and MS7 master cascade assume every MS2 action is registered.
csDepth: The MS2 action set is large (9 engines) — appending all to z.enum(ACTIONS) in one commit creates a wide merge surface; the round-trip E2E must iterate every new action against the real SDK boundary, not spot-check.

Feature-cascade fan-out for surface engines must wire to both prism_cadautomation and any geometry-consuming dispatcher; a one-of-N wiring satisfies the zero-orphan hook but still leaves a dead path the integration test will not exercise unless explicitly enumerated.

csKnowledge: Euler-Poincaré characteristic check for manifold validity
watertight / non-manifold edge detection (each edge bounds exactly 2 faces)
pass1.buildNote: Manifold/watertight validation checks every edge bounds exactly two faces and the Euler characteristic holds — fail loud naming the offending edge/vertex, never return a soft pass.

pass2.systemImpact: BRepTopologyValidatorEngine is the gatekeeper for every MS2-produced solid before CAM — CADValidationGateHook (U-DACAV09) blocks CAM on its PASS, and CADCAMHandoffEngine (MS7) chains its receipt. A soft-pass on a non-manifold solid lets a defective part reach toolpath generation, where it gouges; a false-fail stalls the whole CAD→CAM pipeline. It is the highest-leverage safety engine in MS3.
csDepth: Euler-Poincaré (V−E+F = 2(s−h) with shells s and handles h) is necessary but not sufficient — a solid can satisfy it and still be non-manifold at a single shared vertex; the per-edge 'exactly 2 faces' check and a non-manifold-vertex check (umbrella test) must both run.

B-rep traversal must handle large face counts without stack overflow — iterative DFS with an explicit stack, not recursion (the documented spread→push system-viz fix class); watertightness on a tessellated mesh additionally needs an exact float-tolerance for vertex welding or coincident vertices read as a crack.

pass1.buildNote: Dimensional validation compares actual geometry against spec tolerance bands — every out-of-band feature must be reported individually with its measured value and limit.

pass2.systemImpact: DimensionalValidatorEngine compares produced geometry against the ASME Y14.5 spec from TechnicalDrawingSynthesisEngine (U-DACFS12) and PdfBlueprintDimensionExtractor — its verdict feeds the CADValidationGateHook and the AGIvsHuman benchmark scorecard (MS7). A wrong datum reference or tolerance-band off-by-one passes an out-of-spec part or fails an in-spec one, directly corrupting the beat-humans metric.
csDepth: Tolerance-band comparison must use the GD&T datum-reference frame, not the model coordinate frame — measuring a feature without first establishing its datums (a 3-2-1 fixturing transform) yields a measurement that is numerically precise but references the wrong origin.

Spec-vs-actual diffing must report each out-of-band feature individually with measured value and limit (R12) — a single rolled-up max-deviation hides which feature failed and makes the regression non-actionable; floating-point comparison needs an explicit epsilon tied to the tolerance grade.

csKnowledge: rule-based DFM checking (wall thickness, draft angle, undercut detection)
geometric heuristic scoring per manufacturability rule
pass1.buildNote: A full DFM sweep runs every manufacturability rule and aggregates findings — each rule must fire independently and report concrete violations, not a single rolled-up score.

pass2.systemImpact: ManufacturabilityValidatorEngine runs the full DFM rule sweep — its findings gate whether a design proceeds to CAM and feed the CADValidationGateHook. A rule that silently no-fires (wall thickness, draft, undercut) lets an unmanufacturable feature through; aggregating into one score instead of per-rule findings makes a real DFM violation invisible. CAM strategy selection downstream assumes DFM has already filtered impossible features.
csDepth: Each DFM rule must fire independently and report concrete violations (R12) — a single rolled-up manufacturability score is the anti-pattern; the aggregation should be a list of findings, with the score derived from it, never the score alone.

Tool-reach/accessibility analysis is a visibility problem: a feature is accessible if a tool axis exists that reaches it without collision — this is a configuration-space query, computationally heavy, and must be bounded (sampled tool orientations) or it dominates the sweep cost.

pass1.buildNote: Assembly interference uses BVH broad-phase then exact narrow-phase intersection — every colliding body pair must be reported; a missed collision is a P0 safety defect.

pass2.systemImpact: AssemblyInterferenceValidatorEngine detects collisions between assembly bodies through their motion envelopes (from AssemblyConstraintEngine U-DACFS09) — a missed collision is a P0 safety defect that reaches the shop floor. Its verdict feeds the CADValidationGateHook and is a precondition for fixture/setup planning in MS7. Shares collision-detection infrastructure with the CAM toolpath collision engines.
csDepth: BVH broad-phase must be rebuilt or refit when bodies move through their motion envelope — a static BVH built once misses collisions in non-rest configurations; sweeping the envelope and testing at discrete poses needs a step fine enough to not tunnel a thin body through another.

Narrow-phase solid-solid intersection on tessellated meshes is triangle-triangle testing — exact predicates are needed near coplanar triangles, and the result must be every colliding pair, not first-hit, since reporting one collision hides the rest.

csKnowledge: validation-receipt state lookup before allowing CAM
pass1.buildNote: A blocking hook must signal via stdout JSON, never exit-2 (Windows pipe truncation silently bypasses it); block CAM unless a fresh CAD-validation PASS receipt exists, and fail loud on a missing receipt.

pass2.systemImpact: CADValidationGateHook is the hard fail-closed barrier between CAD and CAM — it blocks every CAM action unless a fresh BRep/dimensional/manufacturability/interference PASS receipt exists. If it regresses (exit-2 instead of stdout-JSON, or accepts a stale receipt), every defective CAD model from MS2/MS3 reaches CAM unchecked. It is the enforcement counterpart of CADCAMHandoffEngine (MS7 U-DAE2E03) and must be in a no-disable hook tier.
csDepth: A blocking PreToolUse hook MUST signal via stdout JSON, not exit-2 — Windows pipe truncation on exit-2 silently bypasses the block (documented task-freshness-gate class); the hook must also exit 0 from a bundled sub-hook position.

Receipt freshness is a TTL problem with a clock-skew hazard: a receipt must carry a content hash of the validated geometry, not just a timestamp — a timestamp-only receipt passes if CAD geometry changed but the validator was not re-run; fail-closed means a missing or unparseable receipt blocks.

csKnowledge: dispatcher action registration with round-trip E2E
pass1.buildNote: Wire every MS3 validator engine to all consuming dispatchers in one commit; the action enum must list each new action — MockMCPServer bypasses the enum gate so verify against the real SDK boundary.

pass2.systemImpact: This unit wires the 4 MS3 validator engines plus the gate hook into prism_cadautomation — until it lands, the validators are unreachable and the CAD→CAM safety chain is open. A missed enum entry 500s the validation action in production while mock tests pass, defeating the entire MS3 safety milestone.
csDepth: Validator-engine fan-out must reach every dispatcher that triggers a CAD→CAM transition, not just prism_cadautomation — a partial wiring leaves a CAM entry path that skips validation.

MockMCPServer bypasses the z.enum(ACTIONS) gate, so a missing-from-enum action 9/9-passes in test while production is 100% broken — the round-trip E2E must hit the real SDK enum boundary (documented recurring false-green class).

csKnowledge: per-moment strategy selection (decision policy over machining state)
greedy vs lookahead strategy choice at each toolpath moment
pass1.buildNote: StrategyPerMoment selects the optimal strategy for each instant of cut given live context — the selector must be deterministic for identical state and verifiable against known reference scenarios.

pass2.systemImpact: StrategyMomentSelectorEngine ('strategy per moment') is the decision policy OptimalToolpathAtMomentEngine (U-CAMAGI03) drives at every cut instant — its choices flow into the full adaptive orchestrator (U-CAMAGI06) and the JM-Die 100-part regression suite (U-CAMAGI15). A non-deterministic selector breaks reproducibility of every downstream CAM-AGI test; a wrong context key picks a strategy that gouges or runs slow.
csDepth: Determinism for identical machining state is a hashing-discipline requirement: the context key must be a canonical, order-stable serialization of the state — a key built from object iteration order or floating-point state without quantization gives different selections on re-run.

Greedy per-moment selection can be globally suboptimal — a bounded lookahead (sample the next k moments) trades cost for quality; the lookahead depth must be a tuned parameter, and the value function must be consistent so greedy and lookahead agree at depth 0.

csKnowledge: orchestration pipeline staging (sub-engine fan-out and merge)
cost-function minimization at each path segment
pass1.buildNote: The core orchestrator composes sub-engines and picks the optimal toolpath per moment — verify the orchestration order and that every sub-engine result is consumed, not silently dropped.

pass2.systemImpact: OptimalToolpathAtMomentEngine is the core orchestration of MS4 CAM-AGI — it composes the strategy selector, variability integrator, and parameter engines into the per-moment toolpath decision. The CAMAGIOrchestratorEngine (U-CAMAGI14) sits above it and the adaptive loop (U-CAMAGI06) wraps it. A dropped sub-engine result silently degrades toolpath quality; a wrong orchestration order uses stale context.
csDepth: Sub-engine fan-out then merge is a dataflow-ordering problem — every sub-engine result must be consumed (R12), not silently dropped; an explicit result-completeness assertion catches a sub-engine that returned nothing.

Optimal-toolpath search over candidate strategies is a cost-minimization with a potentially large branching factor — memoizing identical (state, strategy) evaluations and pruning dominated candidates early keeps it tractable per moment.

csKnowledge: live drift estimation (Kalman filter / EWMA state tracking)
pass1.buildNote: Realtime variability integration tracks live machining drift and compensates — the estimator must converge and never amplify noise; verify with a known synthetic drift profile.

pass2.systemImpact: RealtimeVariabilityIntegratorEngine estimates live machining drift and feeds compensation into LOCDynamicParameterEngine (U-CAMAGI05) and the adaptive orchestrator (U-CAMAGI06). An estimator that amplifies noise drives the closed loop unstable — a divergent compensation command is a machine-safety hazard, so it must be S(x)-gated and route through prism_safety.
csDepth: A Kalman filter or EWMA estimator must be tuned for convergence and noise rejection — an overly-aggressive gain amplifies sensor noise into the compensation command; verify with a known synthetic drift profile that the estimate converges and does not oscillate.

Real-time sensor integration has a sample-rate / latency coupling: a compensation computed on stale sensor data lags the true drift — the loop must bound estimator latency and the integrator must handle missing/late samples without diverging.

csKnowledge: length-of-cut to parameter mapping (interpolation table / regression)
realtime parameter recomputation per LOC change
pass1.buildNote: LOC-driven dynamic parameters recompute feeds/speeds per length-of-cut change — import physics constants from constants.ts, never inline kc/Taylor values.

pass2.systemImpact: LOCDynamicParameterEngine maps length-of-cut changes to live feed/speed parameters consumed by the adaptive orchestrator and ultimately commanded to the machine. An inline kc/Taylor value here is the exact CALC-HARDEN bug class (U-CH01/CH16 enforce against it); a wrong LOC→param transfer function commands a feed the AdaptiveSafetyEnvelopeEngine (MS5 U-DAAE07) must then clamp.
csDepth: Interpolation-table vs regression choice matters: a sparse LOC table needs interpolation that does not overshoot between knots (monotone cubic, not natural spline) — overshoot produces a feed spike at an unsampled LOC.

Realtime recomputation per LOC change must be bounded-latency and idempotent — recomputing on an unchanged LOC must return the identical parameter, or the feed command jitters; physics constants must be imported from constants.ts, never inlined.

csKnowledge: convergence/stability guarantee for the adaptive loop
pass1.buildNote: The full adaptive loop must terminate — bound iterations and verify the loop converges; an unbounded adaptive loop is a hang risk.

pass2.systemImpact: VariabilityAdaptiveOrchestratorEngine is the full sense-decide-act-verify loop for MS4 — it wraps the per-moment toolpath engine and the variability integrator. An unbounded loop is a hang risk that stalls the whole CAM-AGI pipeline; the CAMAGIOrchestratorEngine (U-CAMAGI14) and MS5's master closed loop depend on this loop terminating.
csDepth: A closed adaptive loop MUST have a hard iteration bound AND a convergence criterion — bounding iterations alone can return a non-converged result; convergence-only without a bound is a hang; both are required (the documented adaptive-loop-termination class).

Loop stability needs a contraction guarantee or a damping factor — an adaptive loop whose correction overshoots oscillates; verify the loop converges on a known scenario before claiming it works (R12).

pass1.buildNote: Pareto optimization returns the non-dominated set — verify dominance relation correctness; a candidate dominated on all objectives must never enter the front.

pass2.systemImpact: MultiObjectiveStrategyOptimizerEngine produces the Pareto front of CAM strategies that CycleTimeOptimizer/CostOptimizedStrategy engines and the CAM-AGI orchestrator select from. A wrong dominance relation lets a strictly-dominated candidate into the front, so a downstream consumer can pick a strategy worse on every objective. Feeds the strategy-selection layer of the whole MS4 milestone.
csDepth: Non-dominated sorting (NSGA-II) is O(MN^2) in objectives M and population N — for many candidates a fast non-dominated sort or a dominance-tree is needed; the dominance test itself must be strict (a candidate dominated on all objectives never enters the front, R-correctness).

Weighted-sum scalarization cannot reach concave regions of the Pareto front — epsilon-constraint or NSGA-II is required for a true front; mixing scalarization methods inconsistently across calls produces an unstable front.

pass1.buildNote: Cycle-time optimization minimizes total machining time within physics limits — sum cutting/rapid/dwell time components and verify against a measured baseline part.

pass2.systemImpact: CycleTimeOptimizerEngine minimizes total machining time — its output feeds CostOptimizedStrategyEngine (cost depends on time) and the AGIvsHuman benchmark (cycle time is a headline metric). A cycle-time decomposition that omits tool-change or dwell under-reports time, inflating the beat-humans scorecard with a fabricated win.
csDepth: Cycle time is a sum of decomposed components (cutting + rapid + tool-change + dwell) — each must be a real computed term verified against a measured baseline part; omitting any term is the silent-undercount class.

Rapid-move minimization (air-cut reduction) is a TSP-like ordering problem over toolpath segments — exact TSP is intractable, so a heuristic (nearest-neighbor + 2-opt) is used; the optimization must never reorder cutting moves, only rapids, or it changes the part.

csKnowledge: Taylor tool-life equation (VcT^n = C) wear modeling
pass1.buildNote: Wear-conscious CAM uses the canonical Taylor model — import the Taylor exponent/constant from constants.ts; an inline exponent is the exact CALC-HARDEN bug class.

pass2.systemImpact: ToolLifeAwareStrategyEngine biases CAM strategy by predicted tool wear — its remaining-useful-life estimates feed the cost optimizer (tool cost per part) and tool-change scheduling. An inline Taylor exponent is the precise CALC-HARDEN U-CH01 bug class; a wrong wear model picks a strategy that wears the tool out mid-part, a safety and scrap hazard.
csDepth: The Taylor equation VcT^n = C must import n and C from constants.ts per ISO material group — an inline exponent is the documented CALC-HARDEN defect; the canonical-constants enforcer hook (U-CH16) blocks it.

Wear-rate integration along the toolpath is path-history-dependent — RUL must accumulate wear over engaged segments, not assume uniform wear; a stateless per-segment estimate ignores cumulative damage.

pass1.buildNote: Total-cost optimization sums machine-time, tooling, labor and energy cost — every cost term must be a real engine output, not a hardcoded rate; import sustainability constants.

pass2.systemImpact: CostOptimizedStrategyEngine sums machine/tool/labor/energy cost into a total-cost-of-ownership figure that the CAM-AGI orchestrator and quote-to-ship pipeline consume. A hardcoded rate instead of a real engine output (cycle time, tool life, energy) makes the cost figure fiction — and quoting downstream prices a job on it.
csDepth: Total-cost-of-ownership must compose real engine outputs (cycle time from U-CAMAGI08, tool life from U-CAMAGI09, energy from the sustainability engine) — every cost term sourced, never a hardcoded rate (R12 honesty).

Constrained cost minimization must respect physics limits as hard constraints — minimizing cost by exceeding a feed/torque limit is invalid; the minimizer searches only the feasible region the safety envelope defines.

csKnowledge: strategy normalization to a common taxonomy across CAMs
transfer-learning of strategy knowledge between CAM systems
pass1.buildNote: Cross-CAM transfer synthesizes the best strategy across all CAM systems — strategies must be normalized to one taxonomy before comparison, else apples-to-oranges selection.

Macro parameterization is a variable-binding problem: the differing tokens between call sites become arguments — the binding must be exact and order-stable; a wrong argument-to-position mapping is undetectable by line count but changes the geometry.

CALC-HARDEN-MS0::U-CH01.title: Fix Taylor exponent in MonteCarloEngine, AdaptiveCalibrationEngine, CryogenicCuttingEngine

dimensional consistency check across engine equations
pass1.buildNote: Fix the Taylor exponent placement in MonteCarlo/AdaptiveCalibration/Cryogenic engines — verify against the canonical Taylor constant and a known analytical tool-life value.

Fixing three engines at once needs a regression oracle that fails on a revert of ANY of the three — a single shared invariant test is stronger than three independent ones because it catches a partial fix.

csDepth: Analytical cutter-contact computation is an offset/tangency problem — the CC point is where the tool surface is tangent to the part surface; this has a closed-form solution for standard tool shapes and must be verified against it, not a numerical approximation.

csKnowledge: per-segment force/temperature/deflection simulation along a toolpath
numerical integration of physics state along the path
pass1.buildNote: The novel-toolpath simulator computes force/temp/deflection per path segment — import physics constants from constants.ts; verify each against a known analytical cut.

An inline physics constant is the CALC-HARDEN bug class (U-CH16 blocks it); a wrong per-segment force estimate mis-predicts where a toolpath overloads the tool or deflects the part.
csDepth: Per-segment force/temp/deflection simulation is numerical integration of physics state along the path — the step size must be fine enough to resolve engagement changes; a coarse step misses a brief overload spike.

Engagement-driven cutting-force integration must read the actual radial/axial engagement per segment (from the engagement-geometry engine); physics constants (kc, thermal) must be imported from constants.ts, never inlined.

csKnowledge: voxel grid material-removal tracking (boolean subtraction per move)
pass1.buildNote: Voxel stock integration subtracts the swept tool volume per move — verify removed-material volume against analytical MRR; voxel resolution must be fine enough to not miss thin cuts.

pass2.systemImpact: VoxelStockIntegration tracks material removal by subtracting the swept tool volume per move — the in-process stock model it maintains is consumed by the toolpath simulator (engagement depends on remaining stock) and by collision/rest-machining detection. A too-coarse voxel grid misses thin cuts, so the stock model diverges from reality and engagement/force estimates downstream are wrong.
csDepth: Voxel material-removal is a 3D occupancy-grid update — boolean subtraction of the swept tool volume per move; the grid resolution must be fine enough that no machined feature is thinner than a voxel, or thin cuts are silently missed (memory cost is O(n^3) in resolution — a real space/accuracy tradeoff).

Swept-volume voxelization per move is the per-segment cost driver — an exact swept solid is expensive; conservative voxelization (mark any voxel the swept volume touches) is safe for collision but over-removes for MRR, so the two uses need different rasterization.
